rows.text: Cannot act alone: nothing is done here until the rest of the council agrees.
Does not set the prices or the wages of the trades; for anything touching them, the seat must deal with the guild.
Has no say over the church or its clergy; whatever the seat wants from the faith, it must ask for.
There is coin for the everyday work and little over; any new building or hire means asking the households for more.
The coffers bear the everyday work and more, but every new cost must still be argued for before those who pay it.
Has no paid hands to see its word kept; what the seat decides, the neighbours must be willing to carry out.
Its word is kept by the paid watch, and every extra round the watch walks comes out of the same purse.
Rules by custom alone; a household that will not listen must be talked round, not made to.
Cannot push through anything the strongest power in the place sets itself against; here that power outweighs the seat.
Needs the other powers of the place on its side for anything large; the seat leads, but not alone.
Does not judge the hard cases itself; those go to the court, and the court decides them in its own way.
Can set the market days and the tolls, but cannot make buyers come or sellers stay.
In a place this large the seat sees little for itself; it must act on what its people bring it.
Cannot please everyone at once; whatever the seat gives one side, another asks for next.
Cannot raise more hands or more pay without the council, and in quiet years the council is careful with coin.
Must keep {house} fed and paid out of what the seat allows, and the seat allows what quiet years seem to need.
The walls want upkeep every year; the coin for it has to be asked for, and in quiet years it comes slowly.
The place can afford its guard, but while nothing threatens, every extra hand must be argued for.
There is enough for the hands already under arms and little over; a larger force would mean new dues.
Much of its strength is neighbours who turn out when called, and they have fields and trades to get back to.
Hired companies are paid by the season, and keeping them on when nothing threatens is hard to argue for.
Answers to the seat for every hand and every coin; it cannot set its own numbers.
Must share the coin for keeping order with the paid watch, and it is the watch that people see every day.
In a place this large, those under arms are spread thin across many streets.
Drill keeps hands ready but not keen; quiet years wear on discipline.
Keeping {house} in repair takes alms, and alms come slowly when nothing troubles people.
Does not rule here; whatever the faith wants of the council, it must ask for.
Has few hands to help; in a place this small most of the faith's work falls to one person.
The priests under it answer in name, but each keeps their own flock and their own ways.
The faithful give well in good years, but gifts come with the givers' wishes attached.
Cannot command belief, only ask for it; what it has is what people choose to give.
The work is the same each week and each year, and doing it well earns thanks but little say.
Oaths and marriages are the faith's to bless, but quarrels over them go before the court.
Must see to the faith's own people as well as its flock, and both expect the same patience.
What {house} can take on is limited to what the leading house leaves alone.
The best of the {export} trade is already spoken for; the smaller houses take what is left.
Must keep to the guild's rules on prices and hands, rules the bigger houses had more say in writing.
Sells on the same market days as the leading house, and buyers go to the bigger name first.
Has less coin than the bigger houses to wait on a slow buyer, so it takes smaller, quicker deals.
In good years there is custom enough for all, but the best of it goes to the leading house first.
In a place this large there are many small houses after the same custom.
Has little voice when the council sets the dues on trade; the leading house speaks first.
Does not set the dues on trade; the council does, and the council hears every house.
Lives on the place's trade in {export}; whatever cuts that trade cuts this house first.
Must buy in {import} like everyone else, at prices set somewhere else.
Being first in the trade means being the one every complaint about prices is brought to.
Must keep the smaller houses of the guild content; the guild's rules bind the leading house too.
Runs {house} on what the seat allots it, and must ask before spending more.
Answers to the council for every coin and every choice; little is left to the post's own judgment.
Can do only what the seat has given the post to do; anything more must be asked for.
The purse is sound in good years, but every coin the post spends is counted by someone above it.
Has enough to do the work and no more; there is nothing spare for doing it better.
Must keep {house} paid for out of fees and patrons, and patrons want a say in the work.
Must answer to the council for what is cast within the place.
A spell gone wrong is remembered longer than a hundred done right; the casters' good name is always at stake.
Some people here will not buy a spell at any price, and no fair dealing changes their minds.
Has no seat on the council by right; what the family wants, it must win through friends there.
The old honours of {house} still stand, but the seat decides what those honours are worth.
Old rights count only as far as people still honour them, and fewer remember why they should.
The family's wealth is in land and name, and neither turns into coin quickly.
Cannot get the council to agree on any remedy, and cannot act without it.
Has no paid hands to make its word stick; it must win people back one household at a time.
In a place this small, every attempt to take charge again is watched and talked over by everyone.
Every order that goes unanswered makes the next one easier to ignore.
Every coin spent on the walls is a coin not spent on relief, and both are wanted.
Cannot raise the dues without the council, and the council knows the households cannot pay more.
Must still buy in {import}, and that comes first, before any repair or relief.
Can promise little and pay for less, and every refusal is remembered.
Keeping {house} in repair and feeding the poor draw on the same thin purse.
Can give only what it is given, and in lean years less is given.
In a place this small, everyone knows who the alms went to and who went without.
The church's roof and the poor box both want coin, and there is not enough for both.
Has no hands to enforce anything it settles; its word holds only while people choose to keep it.
Every quarrel it settles is one the council failed to settle, and the council knows it.
Whatever it says of the seat, part of the congregation will have hoped for the other answer.
The council wants its word on the seat; giving it, or holding it back, both cost the faith friends.
Cannot carry the council on anything hard while so many doubt the seat's right.
Must answer for every choice twice: once to those who back the seat, once to those who doubt it.
